summary: Upper KS2 learners study the nervous system as the body's fast communication network with two parts: the central nervous system (brain + spinal cord) that processes and decides, and the peripheral nerves branching to the body that carry messages IN (sensory) and OUT (motor). The signature idea is the reflex arc — for danger the message takes a spinal-cord shortcut (stimulus → sensory nerve → spinal cord → motor nerve → muscle) so the body reacts BEFORE the brain consciously feels or decides. Teaching emphasises SPEED and the shortcut, contrasts a reflex with a considered (brain-routed) action, and builds on the KS1 sense→brain→muscle loop by adding the spinal cord as a fast router.
misconceptions: 'The brain does everything / all messages go to the brain first' — missing the spinal-cord reflex shortcut that bypasses conscious thought.
'Reflexes are just fast decisions' — missing that they are automatic and don't wait for the brain to decide.
'You feel the pain and THEN pull away' — reversed; the reflex pulls you away first, the feeling arrives after.
'Nerves are the same as veins/blood vessels' — confusing the nervous network with the circulatory one; nerves carry signals, not blood.
'Signals travel like something physically running along' slowly — underestimating the near-instant speed of nerve signals.
'The spinal cord is just for holding you up' — missing its role as part of the CNS that routes reflexes and carries messages.

activities.title: Race the signal: the reflex-arc pathway
steps: Trace the pathway of a danger signal: a hand touches a hot pan, a signal travels up the sensory nerve to the spinal cord, and straight back down the motor nerve to the muscle so the hand recoils.
Follow a second signal that continues up to the brain, where the 'ouch!' registers a beat LATER than the hand has already moved.
Use a toggle or comparison to contrast a reflex (spinal-cord shortcut, automatic) with a deliberate action such as deciding to wave, whose signal routes all the way up to the brain and back.
Compare the timing of the two paths using the simulation's or model's timing readout to see the reflex path is faster (a real reflex is too quick to time accurately with a hand-held stopwatch).
State in your own words why the hand moves before the pain is felt.
activities.insight: The nervous system is one network, but a danger message takes a spinal-cord shortcut that fires the muscle before the brain consciously feels or decides — which is why reflexes are automatic and fast and protect us.

activities.title: Feel your own reflexes
steps: Observe or experience a safe real reflex, such as the knee-jerk when the leg is tapped gently just below the kneecap. Recall a time you pulled your hand away from something hot, but do not recreate it.
After a reflex such as the doctor's knee tap (where the leg kicks with no decision), explain what that tells you about where the message went.
Describe whether you chose to make the movement happen, and what that shows about the reflex arc.
activities.insight: Reflexes are automatic and happen without a conscious decision, giving first-hand evidence that the response does not wait for the thinking brain.

activities.title: Map and sort the nervous system
steps: On a body map, identify the central nervous system (brain + spinal cord) and the peripheral nerves branching to the body.
Sort or label parts as central vs peripheral.
Identify which messages travel IN to the CNS (sensory) and which travel OUT to muscles (motor); note that a single nerve in the body often carries both kinds of message.
Distinguish nerves (which carry fast signals) from blood vessels (which carry blood) — they are different networks.
activities.insight: The nervous system splits cleanly into central and peripheral parts, with sensory nerves carrying signals in and motor nerves carrying signals out, and is distinct from the circulatory system.

activities.title: Consolidation questions
steps: Put the reflex-arc steps in order: stimulus → sensory nerve → spinal cord → motor nerve → muscle.
Categorise given body parts as central or peripheral.
Answer why the hand moves before the pain is felt, explaining the spinal-cord-shortcut reason rather than 'you decided to move' or 'the brain thought it was hot first'.
Transfer the idea to the knee-jerk case: explain where the message went.
activities.insight: Learners can independently sequence the arc, classify parts, and justify the before-you-feel-it timing by the bypassed-brain shortcut rather than by vague speed alone.

activities.title: Talk it through: why before you think?
steps: Respond to the prompt: 'You touch something scalding and your hand jerks away BEFORE you feel the pain or decide to move — how can your hand pull back faster than you can think?'
Explain the path the message takes, in full.
Answer follow-ups: Do you still feel the pain afterwards, and why does it arrive a moment later? Why is it USEFUL that this happens without waiting for you to think?
activities.insight: Articulating the pathway and the usefulness of the shortcut forces the bypassed-brain idea to surface rather than a vague 'nerves are fast'.

checkQuestion: You touch something scalding hot and your hand jerks away BEFORE you even feel the pain or decide to move. How can your hand pull back faster than you can think about it? Explain the path the message takes.
checkAnswer: It's a reflex: the message from the skin travels along a sensory nerve to the spinal cord, which sends a message straight back along a motor nerve to the arm muscle to pull away — without waiting to travel up to the thinking part of the brain and back. That short-cut through the spinal cord is why it happens before you consciously feel or decide. The pain signal does reach the brain, but slightly later. Nerve signals travel extremely fast, so it feels instant.
